goal:
# Goal: count Rust, Swift and Lua right

`loc` knows Rust, Swift and Lua only roughly (`src/languages.ts`): Rust's and Swift's block comments
do not nest, raw strings and Lua's long brackets with `=` are unknown, and Rust's `'` is taken for
a string. Lines are miscounted. Teach `loc` each one's real comments and strings, so `countLines`
sorts their lines right (the rule for a line stays: blank, a comment when it holds only comments,
otherwise code). Keep every other language counted as it is now. No new dependencies.

1. **Rust**: `.rs` files, the language `Rust`, a source.
   - `//` line comments (`///` and `//!` too); `/* */` block comments, which nest:
     `/* a /* b */ still a comment */`, over any number of lines.
   - Strings `"…"` with backslash escapes, which may go on over lines; raw strings `r"…"`,
     `r#"…"#`, `r##"…"##` (any number of `#`; the closer is `"` and the same number of `#`; no
     escapes), which may go on over lines; byte strings `b"…"`, `br"…"`, `br#"…"#` likewise.
   - `'` starts a character literal only when one character, or one escape (`'\n'`, `'\''`,
     `'\\'`, `'\u{1F600}'`), and a closing `'` follow it on the line; otherwise it is a lifetime
     or a label (`'a`, `'static`, `'outer:`) and starts nothing.
2. **Swift**: `.swift` files, the language `Swift`, a source.
   - `//` line comments; `/* */` block comments, which nest, as Rust's.
   - Strings `"…"` with backslash escapes, ending on their line; multi-line strings `"""…"""`;
     raw strings `#"…"#` and `#"""…"""#` with any number of `#` (the closer is the quotes and the
     same number of `#`; a backslash escapes nothing unless that many `#` follow it). A `#` not
     followed by more `#` and a `"` starts nothing (`#if`, `#selector`).
3. **Lua**: `.lua` files, the language `Lua`, a source.
   - `--` line comments; long comments `--[[ … ]]` and `--[==[ … ]==]` (any number of `=`; the
     closer has the same number), which may go on over lines. `--[` not followed by `=`s and
     another `[` is a line comment.
   - Strings `"…"` and `'…'` with backslash escapes, ending on their line; long strings `[[ … ]]`
     and `[==[ … ]==]` (the same rule for `=`), which may go on over lines.

facts: src/count.ts holds the only scanner: countLines(text, syntax) splits lines and calls readLine, which carries an `Open { close, comment, escapes }` across lines; closeAt(line, start, close, escapes) finds a closer, and backslash escaping is decided by counting the backslashes in front of it.

readLine checks things in this order at each special character: block openers (syntax.block), then line openers, then multiline delimiters, then single-line strings (syntax.strings, which end at the delimiter or at the end of the line), then regex. Block comments do not nest: an Open closes at the first closer.

specialsOf builds a per-Syntax character class from the first character of every opener and delimiter plus '\\'. Any new kind of opener has to add its start characters there, or the scanner jumps past them.

src/languages.ts: Rust is `source('Rust', { ...C, strings: ["'"], multiline: ['"'] })`, Swift is `source('Swift', { ...C, multiline: ['"""'] })` (so `'` is wrongly treated as a Swift string, through C's QUOTES), and Lua is `const LUA = { line: ['--'], block: [['--[[', ']]']], strings: QUOTES }`, used by `lua: source('Lua', LUA)`.
Syntax is an exported interface (re-exported from src/index.ts) whose fields are all optional, so adding optional fields leaves every other language unchanged.
Tests are in test/count.test.ts and use the helper `count(path, text)`, which goes through languageOf(path)?.syntax. There are no Rust, Swift or Lua tests yet.

Project rules (CLAUDE.md): TypeScript strict with ESM NodeNext, relative imports end in .js, type-only imports use `import type`, vitest tests go in test/*.test.ts and the failing test is written first, `npm run check` must pass before a commit, and no dependencies may be added.
guesses: `npm run check` passes on main today. I couldn't run it because Bash was denied.

Node's RegExp supports lookbehind inside sticky (`y`) patterns, e.g. /(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])b?r(#*)"/y with lastIndex set. This lets Rust's `r` prefix refuse to match inside identifiers. The first workspace should check it in a test.
Swift's single-line raw string `#"…"#` ends on its line, as in Swift itself. The goal doesn't say so, but only `#"""…"""#` is described as going on over lines.
Merges stay conflict-free if the Swift and Lua workspaces each touch only their own lines in src/languages.ts and their own new test file, and leave src/count.ts alone.
ledger.plan: First, one workspace extends the scanner in src/count.ts with block comments that nest and with openers found by a pattern (with counted delimiters, chosen escapes, and lines they may span), and uses that to rewrite Rust. Then two workspaces in parallel give Swift and Lua their new syntax, as data only, on top of it.

nodes.title: Scanner: nested block comments and pattern-delimited tokens; Rust counted right

reviews.summary:
I found no blocker or major defect. I read the diff and `readLine` in src/count.ts, and I did not run the tests (Bash was denied in this session). The reported `npm run check` result is a pass.

- **Nested comments:** `closeAt` tests the closer before the opener, so `/*/` opens a comment and does not close one. The depth carries across lines through `Open.nest`.
- **Delimited tokens:** `delimitedAt` rejects empty matches, so the scan always moves on. Single-line, multiline, whole-token and comment `Delimited`s all take the paths the brief describes.
- **Unchanged languages:** a `Syntax` with neither new field takes the same code paths as before. The new left-to-right escape scan gives the same answers as the old parity count of backslashes.
- **Rust:** the raw-string pattern covers `r"…"`, `r#"…"#` and `br##"…"##`, and the lookbehind keeps `r` from continuing an identifier. `r#ident` stays code. The character-literal pattern covers the escapes the brief lists, `b'x'` works through plain `b`, and a lifetime starts nothing.
- **Interface and tests:** the exports and the `Delimited` and `Syntax` fields match the brief. The tests in test/count.test.ts and test/rust.test.ts cover the cases it names.

nodes.research:
I only read the repo and didn't run anything.

**Layout**
- The code is `src/count.ts` (scanner), `src/languages.ts` (`Syntax`, `GO`, `BY_EXTENSION`) and `src/index.ts`. The only test file is `test/count.test.ts`.
- Its helpers are `count(path, text)` = `countLines(text, languageOf(path)?.syntax)` and `lines(...rows)`. Reuse that style for hand-made `Syntax` objects, calling `countLines(text, syntax)` directly.
- `test/rust.test.ts` is new. Check `count.test.ts` for existing `.rs` cases (grep `a.rs`), because dropping `strings: ["'"]` may change them.
- Scripts: `npm run check` runs `tsc -p tsconfig.json && vitest run`. ESM imports need `.js`.

**Current Rust**
- Line 112: `rs: source('Rust', { ...C, strings: ["'"], multiline: ['"'] })`.
- Replace it with `rs: source('Rust', RUST)`, and put `const RUST` next to `GO` (line 34).
- `src/index.ts` line 2 becomes `export { languageOf, type Delimited, type Language, type Syntax }`.

**Scanner (`readLine` in `src/count.ts`)**
- `Open` is `{close, comment, escapes: boolean}`. Change it to something like `{close, comment, escape: string, nest?: {opener, depth}}`.
  - Use `escape: ''` for none, `'\\'` for backslash, and `'\\##'` for Swift.
  - `escapes` is used in three places: the block open at line 104, the multiline open at line 113, and `closeAt` at lines 81 and 121.
- `closeAt` counts backslashes backwards, which can't handle a multi-character escape. Rewrite it as a forward scan from `start`:
  - If `startsWith(escape, k)`, skip `escape.length + 1`.
  - Else if `startsWith(close, k)`, return at that position.
  - Otherwise advance one character.
  - For nesting, also check for the opener (depth++) and return only when depth reaches 0.
  - Return depth along with the index, since the depth must carry in `Open` to the next line. Test `*/` before `/*`, or whichever order is correct for `/*/`.
- `specialsOf`: add each `delimited[].starts`. It escapes only `\ ] ^ -`, which is fine for `r`, `b`, `'`, `#`, `[`, `-`. The cache is keyed by `Syntax` in a WeakMap.
- Try `delimited` first in the loop, at line 102 before `block`. Set `d.open.lastIndex = i` and call `d.open.exec(line)`. This needs a sticky regex, and a zero-length match must be rejected to avoid an infinite loop.
- On a match:
  - With `close`: set `open = {close: d.close(m), escape: d.escape?.(m) ?? '', comment: !!d.comment}`.
  - A non-comment sets `code = true`.
  - Non-`multiline` ones must end at the end of the line, like `strings`: call `closeAt` immediately and, if there's no closer, set `i = line.length`. Don't leave `open` set.
  - Without `close`: the whole token is code. Set `i += m[0].length`, `before = last char`, `code = true`, and open nothing.
- On no match, fall through to the existing branches. For example, a `b` or `r` that isn't a raw string must end up as plain code through the generic path at lines 126–136.
- A comment delimited must not set `code`. Carrying over, line 80 only sets code when `!open.comment`.

**Traps**
- Raw strings: use a lookbehind so `r` can't continue an identifier, e.g. `/(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])b?r(#*)"/y`. The lookbehind sees the whole `line` string, so `br#"` is matched once. `r#ident` has no `"`, so it fails and counts as code.
- The closer is `'"' + m[1]`, with no escape and `multiline: true`.
- Char literal regex: `/'(?:[^\\'\n]|\\u\{[0-9a-fA-F_]+\}|\\x[0-9a-fA-F]{2}|\\.)'/y`.
  - With no `close`, `'a` and `'static` fail to match, so `'` starts nothing.
  - `'"'` is consumed whole, so the `"` isn't read as a string.
  - `<'a, 'b>` is safe: `'a,` has no closing `'` right after the one character.
- The existing `\\` special skips two characters in plain code (line 136). Keep that.
- `"` strings in Rust: keep `multiline: ['"']`. They have escapes because `raw` doesn't list `"`.
- Don't give `RUST` any `strings`.
- Everything new is optional, so syntaxes without the fields behave as now. Existing tests must stay green.

nodes.title: Swift: nested comments, multi-line and raw strings
nodes.brief:
Starting from the scanner-rust branch, change only the Swift lines of src/languages.ts: add `const SWIFT` just after `JSON_SYNTAX` and point `swift: source('Swift', SWIFT)` at it. Add a new test/swift.test.ts, written first. Do not touch src/count.ts; scanner-rust already provides `Syntax.nested` and `Syntax.delimited` (`Delimited { starts, open, close?, escape?, comment?, multiline? }`, tried before everything else, first match wins). If a real gap in the scanner turns up, report it rather than working around it.

SWIFT is as follows. `line: ['//']`, `block: [['/*','*/']]`, `nested: true`. `strings: ['"']` only: Swift has no `'` strings, so drop C's QUOTES. These strings take backslash escapes and end on their line. `multiline: ['"""']` takes escapes. Raw strings are two Delimiteds starting with `#`, the triple one first. `#"""…"""#` (any number of `#`) is multiline, closes at `"""` plus the same `#`s, and its escape is `\\` plus the same `#`s. `#"…"#` is single-line with the same closer and escape rule. A `#` not followed by more `#`s and a `"` starts nothing (`#if`, `#selector`, `#available`).

Tests: nested block comments over lines; a `"""` string holding `//` and `/*` lines; `#"a\\"#` closing at `"#` (the backslash escapes nothing); `#"a\\#"b"#` where `\\#"` is escaped; `##"…"##`; `#if DEBUG` and `// x` lines; an apostrophe such as `let s = "it's" // c` read as code. `npm run check` must pass.

reviews.summary: The change meets the brief. I read it against the scanner in src/count.ts. I did not re-run `npm run check`; the check output you gave me says it passed. Only the Swift lines of src/languages.ts changed, `SWIFT` sits just after `JSON_SYNTAX`, and `swift: source('Swift', SWIFT)` points at it. src/count.ts is untouched. `strings: ['"']` has dropped `'`. The triple-`#` Delimited comes before the single-line one. A bare `#` such as `#if` or `#selector` matches neither opener, so it starts nothing. The close and escape functions rebuild the right `#`s from the opener's match. Tracing the scanner by hand gives the expected result for each test: `\"#` closes the string, `\#"` is escaped, `##"` closes only at `"##`, and `#"""` closes only at `"""#`. The test file covers every case the brief lists.

nodes.research:
**Base:** `hive/swift` is at 0bc177f, which already has the scanner-rust work. `Syntax.nested`, `Syntax.delimited` and `Delimited` exist in `src/languages.ts:1-50`, and `src/count.ts` reads them. I found no scanner gap, so you shouldn't need to touch `count.ts`.

**What to change in `src/languages.ts`**
- Add `const SWIFT: Syntax` right after `JSON_SYNTAX` (the last const before `source`, around line 82).
- Change line ~130 to `swift: source('Swift', SWIFT)`. It is currently `{ ...C, multiline: ['"""'] }`.
- Use the file's existing style: `RUST` at lines 55-72 is the model, with `...C_COMMENTS`, `nested: true`, and a `delimited` array with comments.

**Suggested shape**
```ts
const SWIFT: Syntax = {
  ...C_COMMENTS, nested: true, strings: ['"'], multiline: ['"""'],
  delimited: [
    { starts: '#', open: /(#+)"""/y, close: m => '"""' + m[1], escape: m => '\\' + m[1], multiline: true },
    { starts: '#', open: /(#+)"/y,   close: m => '"' + m[1],   escape: m => '\\' + m[1] },
  ],
};
```
- The triple form goes first, as the brief says. Use the `uy` flags if you want to match Rust's regex style.
- `#if` and `#selector` don't match `(#+)"`, so they start nothing. `#` is then just code.
- `#` is a special character only because of `delimited.starts`. `specialsOf` adds it automatically.

**Scanner semantics from `count.ts`**
- `delimitedAt` tries delimiters first, and the opener must match at the sticky index.
- `closeAt` checks the escape before the closer. The escape string skips itself plus one character.
- A Delimited without `multiline` ends at its closer or at the end of the line.
- Plain `multiline: ['"""']` is escaped with `\`, since it isn't in `raw`.
- Nested comments carry their depth across lines.
- `strings: ['"']` leaves `'` as plain code, so `"it's" // c` is code.

**Test conventions** (copy `test/rust.test.ts`)
- Header: `import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest'`, `countLines` from `../src/count.js`, and `languageOf` from `../src/languages.js`.
- Helpers: `const lines = (...rows) => rows.join('\n') + '\n'` and `const swift = (...rows) => countLines(lines(...rows), languageOf('a.swift')?.syntax)`.
- Expected values look like `toEqual({ lines, code, comments, blank })`.
- First test: `languageOf('x.swift')` matches `{ name: 'Swift', kind: 'source' }`.
- Write the tests first and watch them fail. Several would already pass under the old syntax, such as `"""`. The nested-comment and `#"…"#` cases should fail.

**Trap: backslash notation in the brief.** The brief writes `#"a\\"#` and `#"a\\#"b"#`, and this is probably markdown escaping.
- The real Swift source for the first is `#"a\"#`. With one `#`, the escape is `\#`, so a bare `\` escapes nothing and the string closes at `"#`.
- The second is `#"a\#"b"#`. Here `\#"` escapes the quote, so the string runs through the final `"#`.
- In a TS test, write these as `'#"a\\"#'` and `'#"a\\#"b"#'`. Put a trailing code or comment token after each string, such as `// c`. Then you can tell whether the string closed: if it did, the `//` is a comment on a code line, and if not, the string is still open and the following lines count as code.
- Add a `##"…"##` case, for example one holding `"#` inside.
- Include `#if DEBUG` and `// x` lines.
- Check that a `"""` block holding `//` and `/*` lines counts as code on every line.

Before committing, run `npm run check`. Don't add dependencies.

nodes.title: Lua: long comments and long strings with = levels
nodes.brief:
Starting from the scanner-rust branch, change only the `const LUA` line of src/languages.ts and add a new test/lua.test.ts, written first. Do not touch src/count.ts; scanner-rust already provides `Syntax.delimited` (`Delimited { starts, open, close?, escape?, comment?, multiline? }`, tried before `block` and `line`, first match wins). If a real gap in the scanner turns up, report it rather than working around it.

LUA is as follows. `line: ['--']` and `strings: QUOTES`, which take backslash escapes and end on their line. Drop the `block` entry. There are two Delimiteds, with no escapes and multiline. First, the long comment: it starts with `-`, its pattern is like /--\[(=*)\[/y, it is a comment, and its closer is `]` plus the same `=`s plus `]`. Second, the long string: it starts with `[`, its pattern is like /\[(=*)\[/y, it is code, and it has the same closer. `--[` not followed by `=`s and another `[` falls through to the `--` line comment.

Tests: `--[[ … ]]` and `--[==[ … ]] still … ]==]` over lines; `--[ not long` as a one-line comment; a `[[` long string holding `--` lines counted as code; `[=[ … ]=]`; `'--'` and `"[["` in ordinary strings; code after a long comment closes on the same line counted as code. `npm run check` must pass.

reviews.summary:
The change matches the brief. Only the `LUA` line in src/languages.ts changed, and test/lua.test.ts was added. src/count.ts is untouched. `npm run check` passed. I traced the scanner for the edge cases the brief names:
- `--[ x` and `--[= x` don't match the long-comment pattern, so they fall through to the `--` line comment.
- `---[[` falls to the line comment, as in Lua.
- Both Delimiteds are multiline and have no escape, so a closer like `]==]` has to carry the same number of `=`s.
- A long string counts as code on every line it spans.
- Code after a long comment closes on the same line counts as code.
- `-` and `[` are now scanner trigger characters, but a lone `-` or `[` that matches no pattern is treated as ordinary code.
I found no defects.

nodes.research:
**Findings**

The `hive/lua` branch (HEAD `0bc177f`) already contains scanner-rust's work. `Syntax.delimited`, `Delimited` and `nested` are all in `src/languages.ts` and `src/count.ts`. Don't touch `src/count.ts`. I found no scanner gap.

**What to change**
- Only the `const LUA` line (`src/languages.ts`, in the `DASHES` / `POWERSHELL` area). It currently reads `{ line: ['--'], block: [['--[[', ']]']], strings: QUOTES }`.
- Replace it with `line: ['--']`, `strings: QUOTES` and no `block`. Add a `delimited` array of two entries, in this order:
  1. The long comment: `starts: '-'`, `open: /--\[(=*)\[/y`, `close: (m) => ']' + m[1] + ']'`, `comment: true`, `multiline: true`. There is no `escape`.
  2. The long string: `starts: '['`, `open: /\[(=*)\[/y`, the same `close`, `multiline: true`. There is no `comment` (so it counts as code) and no `escape`.
- The `Delimited` doc comment in `languages.ts` already mentions Lua, so it needs no edit.

**How the scanner behaves (`src/count.ts`)**
- The `starts` characters become scanner specials automatically (`specialsOf`). `-` and `[` are escaped properly in the character class.
- `delimitedAt` is tried before `block`, `line` and `strings`. It only accepts a match anchored at `i` that isn't empty.
- `--[ not long` fails the long-comment regex, so it falls through to the `--` line comment.
- `--[==[ a ]] b` stays open, since the closer needs the same number of `=`.
- A `'--'` or `"[["` inside an ordinary string is consumed by the string branch, because the opener is found at the quote first. This is fine.
- An open comment sets no `code` flag, so text after the close on the same line (`]] x = 1`) is counted as code. The scan continues after `end`.
- `x = 1 --[[ c` followed by `d ]]` makes line 1 code and line 2 a comment.
- A long string line (`open` non-comment) sets `code = true` on every line, including the continuation lines. So `[[` containing `-- foo` lines counts them as code.
- Lua indexing such as `t[[1]]`, or `a[b[1]]`, matches `\[(=*)\[` only when `[[` is adjacent. That is real Lua long-string syntax anyway.

**Conventions for the test**
- Create `test/lua.test.ts` and write it first. Copy the header of `test/rust.test.ts`:
  - `import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest'`
  - `countLines` from `'../src/count.js'`
  - `languageOf` from `'../src/languages.js'`
  - `const lines = (...rows) => rows.join('\n') + '\n'`
  - `const lua = (...rows) => countLines(lines(...rows), languageOf('a.lua')?.syntax)`
- Assert `{ lines, code, comments, blank }` with `toEqual`.
- Include `expect(languageOf('x.lua')).toMatchObject({ name: 'Lua', kind: 'source' })`.
- Cases to cover:
  - `--[[ … ]]` over lines.
  - `--[==[ … ]] still … ]==]`.
  - `--[ not long` as a one-line comment.
  - A `[[` string holding `--` lines counted as code.
  - `[=[ … ]=]`.
  - `'--'` and `"[["` in ordinary strings.
  - Code after a long comment closes on the same line.
- `test/count.test.ts:225-240` already has an ad-hoc Lua-like comment-delimited test. It doesn't need changing.

**Verification:** `npm run check` runs `tsc -p tsconfig.json` and then `vitest run`. Commit only if asked. If you do, end the message with `Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>`.
